title: Angular Momentum
short_intro: Angular momentum is the rotational analogue of linear momentum, quantifying the rotational inertia and angular velocity of a particle or system. For a point particle, it is defined as the cross product of its position vector and linear momentum vector.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of angular momentum for point masses and rigid bodies, relation with torque, conservation of angular momentum in central force fields, and basic numerical problems involving radius, mass, and velocity.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Angular momentum of systems of particles, relation with moment of inertia and angular velocity (L = Iω), precession, rotating frames, matrices/tensors of inertia for rigid bodies, and quantum mechanical aspects.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Significance
bullets: Angular momentum L of a particle is given by L = r × p = r × (mv).
It depends on the choice of the origin about which the position vector r is measured.
It measures the tendency of an object to continue spinning or revolving around a specific point.

concept_notes.heading: Relation Between Torque and Angular Momentum
bullets: The time rate of change of angular momentum of a particle is equal to the net external torque acting on it: τ_ext = dL/dt.
If the net external torque is zero, the total angular momentum of the system remains constant.
This forms the foundational principle of conservation of angular momentum.

concept_notes.heading: Conservation of Angular Momentum
bullets: In a central force field (such as gravitational or electrostatic forces), the torque due to the force is zero because the force is directed along the position vector.
Consequently, angular momentum per unit mass is conserved, leading directly to Kepler's second law of planetary motion (equal areas swept in equal intervals of time).
Examples include a skater pulling their arms inward to increase rotational speed (ω).

concept_notes.heading: Angular Momentum of a Rigid Body
bullets: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with angular velocity ω, the angular momentum is L = Iω, where I is the moment of inertia about that axis.
If the rotation is not about a principal axis of inertia, the angular momentum vector L and the angular velocity vector ω may not be parallel.
The general relation uses the inertia tensor: L_i = ∑ I_ij ω_j.

derivations.title: Torque and Rate of Change of Angular Momentum
derivations.conditions: Particle of mass m moving with position vector r and linear momentum p under net force F.
steps: Start with the definition of angular momentum: L = r × p.
Differentiate both sides with respect to time t: dL/dt = d(r × p)/dt.
Apply the product rule for differentiation: dL/dt = (dr/dt × p) + (r × dp/dt).
Recognize that dr/dt = v and p = mv, so dr/dt × p = v × mv = 0 since velocity and momentum are collinear.
Substitute dp/dt = F (Newton's second law) into the second term: dL/dt = r × F.
Identify r × F as the net external torque τ.

derivations.title: Conservation of Angular Momentum in Central Force Fields
derivations.conditions: A particle moving under a central force directed toward or away from the origin.
steps: Write the expression for the torque of a central force: τ = r × F = r × f(r)r̂.
Since the unit vector r̂ is parallel to the position vector r, the cross product r × r̂ is zero.
Using the relation dL/dt = τ, we get dL/dt = 0.
Integrate with respect to time to show L is constant.

graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An elliptical orbit with the sun at one focus, showing sector areas swept out in equal time intervals.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates constant areal velocity (dA/dt = L/2m), confirming the conservation of angular momentum under a central gravitational force.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in conceptual questions linking Kepler's second law with angular momentum conservation.

graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A spinning top or gyroscope indicating the spin angular momentum vector L and the precession cone under gravity torque.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass 2 kg is moving with a velocity v = (3i + 4j) m/s at a position r = (1i - 1j) m relative to the origin. Find its angular momentum.
solution_steps: Write the given vectors: r = 1i - 1j and v = 3i + 4j.
Calculate linear momentum p = mv = 2(3i + 4j) = 6i + 8j kg m/s.
Compute the cross product L = r × p using the determinant method: i(1(8) - (-1)(6)) style expansion -> L = (1)(8) - (-1)(6) along k̂.

solved_numericals.question: A planet orbits the Sun in an elliptical path. Its distance at perihelion is 2 × 10^{11} m and speed is 40 km/s. What is its speed at aphelion if the distance from the Sun is 4 × 10^{11} m?
solution_steps: Identify that gravitational force is a central force, so angular momentum is conserved.
Apply conservation of angular momentum: m * v_p * r_p = m * v_a * r_a.
Cancel mass m and substitute values: (40 km/s) * (2 × 10^{11} m) = v_a * (4 × 10^{11} m).

solved_numericals.question: A uniform disc of mass 5 kg and radius 0.2 m is rotating freely about its central axis at 60 rad/s. A small 1 kg mass is gently dropped onto the rim of the disc. What is the new angular velocity of the system?
solution_steps: Calculate the initial moment of inertia of the disc: I_1 = (1/2) M R^2 = 0.5 * 5 * (0.2)^2 = 0.1 kg m².
Calculate the moment of inertia of the added mass at the rim: I_mass = m R^2 = 1 * (0.2)^2 = 0.04 kg m².
Final moment of inertia of the combined system: I_2 = I_1 + I_mass = 0.1 + 0.04 = 0.14 kg m².
Apply conservation of angular momentum: I_1 ω_1 = I_2 ω_2.

assumptions_and_limitations: Angular momentum depends explicitly on the choice of origin; changing the reference origin alters the value of L unless the net external force is zero or parallel to the position vector.
For rigid bodies, the relation L = Iω assumes the body is truly rigid and undergoes rotation about a fixed or principal axis of inertia.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Angular momentum is always parallel to angular velocity for any rotating body.
common_misconceptions.correct: Angular momentum is parallel to angular velocity only when the rotation occurs about a principal axis of inertia.
common_misconceptions.why: For asymmetric bodies, the off-diagonal elements of the inertia tensor cause L and ω to point in different directions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: If the linear momentum of a particle changes, its angular momentum must also change.
common_misconceptions.correct: Linear momentum can change while angular momentum remains constant if the line of action of the force passes through the origin.
common_misconceptions.why: Torque (τ = r × F) determines the change in angular momentum, not force alone.

quick_revision: In central force fields, angular momentum is strictly conserved.
